claims.text: The railway linked the port of Liverpool with textile-industry Manchester, carrying goods and passengers; it was the first modern inter-city passenger railway, relying exclusively on steam with scheduled services and signalling.

After 17 miles the engines stopped for water at Newton-le-Willows; Huskisson left his carriage and approached Wellington to reconcile after earlier disagreements.
Rocket, driven by Joseph Locke, approached on the adjacent track and struck Huskisson, badly mangling his leg; George Stephenson drove him by train to Eccles.
Despite calls to return to Liverpool, the party proceeded to Manchester, where a large crowd awaited; the mood was subdued, but the reception and banquet were to go ahead.
Huskisson died at around 9 p.m. after being mortally wounded.

claims.text: Rivalry between Meiji Japan and Qing China over Korea coincided with the Donghak Peasant Rebellion. In June 1894 Korea requested Chinese troops; Japan also dispatched forces, citing protection of its legation and residents.
At Pungdo on 25 July 1894, Japanese and Chinese ships fought their first naval engagement; the British-registered transport Kowshing, carrying Chinese reinforcements, was sunk.
The first land engagement occurred at Seonghwan on 29 July. Emperor Meiji and Qing Emperor Guangxu declared war on 1 August, after the initial battles.
Japanese forces attacked Pyongyang on 15 September; Chinese forces evacuated during the night, and the Japanese occupied the city the following morning.
At the naval Battle of the Yalu River on 17 September, both fleets suffered losses, but Chinese naval power in the Yellow Sea was significantly reduced.

The Donghak Peasant Army mobilised again against Korean government collaboration with Japan. Japanese and Korean government forces inflicted heavy losses on it at Gongju on 28–29 November 1894; sporadic clashes continued into 1895.
Haicheng fell to Japan in December 1894; Chinese attempts to retake it and fighting around the city continued until the end of February 1895.

Japan and Qing China signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki on 17 April 1895. Its terms included Chinese recognition of Korean independence, cession of Liaodong, Taiwan and the Pescadores, and an indemnity. Representatives included Itō Hirobumi, Mutsu Munemitsu, Li Hongzhang and Li Jingfang.
After German, Russian and French objections to the Liaodong cession, Japan returned the peninsula to China under a further treaty on 18 November 1895.
Despite the April peace treaty, organised fighting over Taiwan's cession to Japan continued until November 1895.
